dialogues.speaker: Nicole
dialogues.text: Yes, just like that... This will be more than enough to assassinate Varka.

choices.text: I heard you the first time!

response.speaker: Nicole
response.text: I need ideas for "Assassinating the Grand Master."

choices.text: I'm going to report this to Alice, you know...

response.speaker: Nicole
response.text: I went over this with Alice a long while ago. She stands with me, and has even offered several ideas on how I might take him out.

response.speaker: Nicole
response.text: Of all her suggestions, this one seemed most promising... Bring a full cart of Mondstadt's newest Dandelion Wine all the way here... And then, before Varka's very eyes, tip the entire cart over the cliff.

response.speaker: Nicole
response.text: Perhaps the monumental, overwhelming grief will make him collapse — or go drown himself in whatever other wine he can find.

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: That doesn't sound like it'll work... Wait, no! Don't even think about doing something so horrible!

response.speaker: Nicole
response.text: When writing a novel, the author, naturally, seeks to be as extravagant as possible. Especially when writing detective novels. If the opening lacks a striking turn, how is the rest of the plot meant to unfold?

response.speaker: Nicole
response.text: Alas, this will be my final attempt at writing detective novels... Oh, I suppose they call them crime novels in Inazuma. In any case, they all tell of crime — there's hardly a meaningful distinction.

response.speaker: Nicole
response.text: I also discussed it with Barbie, but our novel-writing sessions always evolve into crime-planning sessions. Methods of crime and puzzles of deduction — we have explored plenty of those, yet the plot would not advance.

response.speaker: Player
response.text: Such as...

response.speaker: Nicole
response.text: The Angel Killer Case. Try as they might, the culprit remained elusive. The desperate detective rushed into the crowd, then shouted the revered names of the "Four Great Rulers" at the sky.

response.speaker: Nicole
response.text: Whoosh... Pitter-patter... Boom. Detective and murderer, reduced to ash.

response.speaker: Paimon
response.text: What kind of writing is that? Doesn't that leave no room for deduction at all!?

response.speaker: Nicole
response.text: Of course there is. It was only through painstaking deduction that the detective finally discovered the names of the "Four Great Rulers," learning also that shouting them at the sky would inevitably reduce one to ash.

response.speaker: Player
response.text: We mean using deduction to find the killer!

response.speaker: Nicole
response.text: My point exactly. Simply deducing who the culprit is has become dreadfully unoriginal. The subject of one's deductions must be something more creative...

response.speaker: Nicole
response.text: I even thought of having a Seelie detective. An angel who, longing to become a detective, became a Seelie, and by some twist of fate, ended up as a detective's assistant.

response.speaker: Nicole
response.text: All Seelies love to guide people, so this one went about leading the detective from case to case... I found the idea rather interesting.

response.speaker: Nicole
response.text: Hmm, come to think of it, "The Seelie Detective and The Angel Killer Case" seem far more interesting than "Assassinating the Grand Master." Never mind, guess I'll move on to work on that idea, then!

choices.text: What happened to all the details you were working through?

response.speaker: Nicole
response.text: It's precisely because I overthink every little detail that I've lost interest in continuing. Not to mention the mountain of words I'll have to write. The very thought of penning all those words... Ugh, what a hassle. And I can't even get a ghostwriter for this one...

response.speaker: Nicole
response.text: I'll just work on the Angel Killer Case instead. But how might the detective deduce the truth? Hmm... Perhaps he could have a conveniently informative dream...

choices.text: You are NOT allowed to hurt the Grand Master—
